Diagrams

A visual language: the kinds of picture an agent draws in its replies, so the author reads at a glance what words would take a page to say. For each kind: what it shows, when it fits and when it does not, its parts, how it is drawn. Which kind for which data: the chooser in the guide Data as a picture.

01Sequence diagram: who talks to whom

The course of events: the parts of a system as columns, what they send each other as arrows, top to bottom in time order. A request, a failure, a retry or a fix reads in one look, and today beside proposed shows only the change.

Fits when

  • Parts pass something along: a person, a browser, a server, a database, a job, an outside service.
  • The order matters: a failure, a retry, a timeout, a race; what happens where, and after what.
  • A fix changes the course: a step added, an event dropped, a call moved. Today beside proposed.

Not when

  • One part alone, nothing passed between: its states are a state diagram, its decisions a flowchart, its look a screenshot.
  • The order does not matter, only where the parts run or how the data links: a container sketch or an entity-relationship diagram.
  • The times matter more than who: a timeline.
  • Too many at once: more than five participants or ten messages. Split it in two, or say it in a table.
  • A change the author sees on screen: screenshots before and after say it better.

How it is drawn

  1. Participants: one column each, a plain icon above a short name. A person, a laptop or browser, a server, a database cylinder, a clock for a cronjob, a page for another writer or a file, a cloud for an outside service, a warning triangle for an error tracker. The icons carry most of the reading; the names stay short.
  2. Lifelines: a dashed vertical line under each participant.
  3. Messages: arrows between lifelines, top to bottom in time order, each with a few words. A request blue, a failure or an error red, a success or an answer green, what stays the same grey. A note on a step sits on its arrow: 13:05 INSERT … SELECT, 403 plan limit.
  4. A step on a clock or a loop (every minute, a retry until it works): a low rectangle with well-rounded corners (48 high for 18-pixel words, its radius a third of that), spanning the lifelines it involves. One arrowhead sits on its top edge pointing right, one on its bottom edge pointing left, so it reads as a cycle. Its period is written inside (every minute); what it checks and does goes beside it, right of the lifelines: alive? writing?, then gone, silent 30 s or older: started again. The loop is orange, the waiting colour; its words keep the usual text colours.

Turned down: a straight arrow reads as one call, not a repeat; an ellipse reads poorly; a UML loop frame around the steps, its tag in the corner, stretches a compact diagram into a long one. A refresh sign, a filled rectangle with an arrow on every side and a path out of a lifeline and back came second. 5. Today beside proposed (or before beside after, today beside made): two framed panels, tagged, the same participants in the same order, so only the change differs. The change is drawn, not described: an event crossed out, a step added, a participant greyed. 6. Around it: a title line with the item's id and what it is, one line of context under it (where, how often), one line of proof under the panels. 7. In the app's colours, and drawn for the width it is shown at: its words no smaller than the text around it.

Examples

In the author's words
  • Pictures that are clear to me; I'd like agents to make pictures of this kind in their messages: it makes them easier to understand. And especially the icons. (2026-10-13 15:29)

# Sequence diagram: who talks to whom

The course of events: the parts of a system as columns, what they send each
other as arrows, top to bottom in time order. A request, a failure, a retry or
a fix reads in one look, and today beside proposed shows only the change.

![Its parts: participants with an icon above the name, dashed lifelines under them, messages as arrows top to bottom; blue a request, green a success, red a failure, grey what stays the same](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_parts.svg)

## Fits when

- **Parts pass something along:** a person, a browser, a server, a database,
  a job, an outside service.
- **The order matters:** a failure, a retry, a timeout, a race; what happens
  where, and after what.
- **A fix changes the course:** a step added, an event dropped, a call moved.
  Today beside proposed.

## Not when

- **One part alone,** nothing passed between: its states are a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md), its decisions a [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md), its
  look a screenshot.
- **The order does not matter,** only where the parts run or how the data
  links: a [container sketch](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/containers.md) or an
  [entity-relationship diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/entities.md).
- **The times matter more than who:** a [timeline](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/timeline.md).
- **Too many at once:** more than five participants or ten messages. Split
  it in two, or say it in a table.
- **A change the author sees on screen:** screenshots before and after say it
  better.

## How it is drawn

1. **Participants:** one column each, a plain icon above a short name. A
   person, a laptop or browser, a server, a database cylinder, a clock for a
   cronjob, a page for another writer or a file, a cloud for an outside
   service, a warning triangle for an error tracker. The icons carry most of
   the reading; the names stay short.
2. **Lifelines:** a dashed vertical line under each participant.
3. **Messages:** arrows between lifelines, top to bottom in time order, each
   with a few words. A request blue, a failure or an error red, a success or
   an answer green, what stays the same grey. A note on a step sits on its
   arrow: `13:05 INSERT … SELECT`, `403 plan limit`.
4. **A step on a clock or a loop** (every minute, a retry until it works):
   a low rectangle with well-rounded corners (48 high for 18-pixel words,
   its radius a third of that), spanning the lifelines it involves. One arrowhead sits on its top
   edge pointing right, one on its bottom edge pointing left, so it reads as
   a cycle. Its period is written inside (`every minute`); what it checks and
   does goes beside it, right of the lifelines: `alive? writing?`, then
   `gone, silent 30 s or older: started again`. The loop is orange, the
   waiting colour; its words keep the usual text colours.

   Turned down: a straight arrow reads as one call, not a repeat; an ellipse
   reads poorly; a UML `loop` frame around the steps, its tag in the corner,
   stretches a compact diagram into a long one. A refresh sign, a filled
   rectangle with an arrow on every side and a path out of a lifeline and
   back came second.
5. **Today beside proposed** (or before beside after, today beside made): two
   framed panels, tagged, the same participants in the same order, so only
   the change differs. The change is drawn, not described: an event crossed
   out, a step added, a participant greyed.
6. **Around it:** a title line with the item's id and what it is, one line of
   context under it (where, how often), one line of proof under the panels.
7. **In the app's colours,** and drawn for the width it is shown at: its words
   no smaller than the text around it.

![S4, a plan limit: today the browser sends an error event to the tracker after the upgrade window; proposed, no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_plan_limit.svg)

## Examples

![servermon kept running by the agent: systemd starts the agent, the agent writes and starts servermon, which writes a JSON line a second and keeps running when the agent restarts; every minute, in an orange rounded loop, the agent asks alive? writing? and starts it again if gone or silent 30 s](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_servermon_loop.svg)

![U2, an upload retried: before, a passing 500 fails the export; after, the job waits and puts the file again, and the export is done](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_upload_retried.svg)

![D1, a deadlock in a cronjob retried inside the run: today an error event and the rows a run later; made, once more at once and no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_deadlock_retried.svg)

![D1, the same deadlock with no change proposed: the retry drawn as what would be done only if it grows](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_deadlock_not_now.svg)

![E7, the exporter's upload: today a failed upload is an error event; proposed, retried up to 3 times, the file arrives, no event](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_exporter_upload.svg)

![One upload through a render service: the browser gets a signed URL from the API through Cloudflare, puts the file straight to S3, asks for a render; the API queues it and answers 202; later SQS starts Lambda, which renders to S3 and marks the job done](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/sequence_banner_render.svg)

02One case: today beside fixed

One real request, its answer today beside its answer with the fix: the question on top, two framed panels under it, red for today and green for the fix. Big numbers and what works and what is missing follow, so the one case stands for the rest.

Fits when

  • One real request shows the gap: a question a help chat cannot answer, a call that fails, a search that finds nothing.
  • The fix is content or data, and its effect is the answer itself: a table, a value, a reply.
  • The author must decide what to do next: the case convinces, the lists say what else is open and what each costs.

Not when

  • The course of messages between parts changes, not the answer: a sequence diagram, today beside proposed.
  • Many parts at once, each with its state: a status dashboard.
  • A change on screen: two screenshots, before and after.

How it is drawn

  1. The question: quoted big in a soft blue box, where it was asked and when in grey beside it. The real words, not a summary.
  2. Today: a red frame, a red cross in a circle and "Today:" with why it fails; inside, the real answer as given and a red tag ("not_covered").
  3. With the fix: a green frame, a green tick and "With" and the fix; inside, the answer it would give and a green tag ("answered"). Values go in a small table, a line between rows.
  4. A verdict under each: in bold, red or green, what the panel shows; a line under it says where the real answer was seen, or in amber what is still to confirm.
  5. KPI cards: four big numbers for the whole, each a few words of what it counts; red or amber for a count that stands for a gap.
  6. Two lists: "Works" with green ticks; "Missing, by effort" with a pill per item, red for work to do (small, medium), amber for what waits on an answer (wait, check, decide). The item the case is about first, in bold.
  7. Ticks and crosses are drawn as paths, not typed as glyphs, so every font shows them alike.
In the author's words
  • Add all of them, only make them anonymous: nothing about the company or anything personal. (2026-10-14 23:56, of the visual-lang drafts)

# One case: today beside fixed

One real request, its answer today beside its answer with the fix: the
question on top, two framed panels under it, red for today and green for
the fix. Big numbers and what works and what is missing follow, so the one
case stands for the rest.

![A shop's help chat asked how much shipping to Canada is: today a vague reply, not covered; with a shipping-rates article, a table of four rates, answered; then the numbers, what works and what is missing, by effort](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/case_shipping.svg)

## Fits when

- **One real request shows the gap:** a question a help chat cannot
  answer, a call that fails, a search that finds nothing.
- **The fix is content or data,** and its effect is the answer itself: a
  table, a value, a reply.
- **The author must decide what to do next:** the case convinces, the
  lists say what else is open and what each costs.

## Not when

- **The course of messages between parts** changes, not the answer: a
  [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md), today beside proposed.
- **Many parts at once,** each with its state: a
  [status dashboard](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/dashboard.md).
- **A change on screen:** two screenshots, before and after.

## How it is drawn

1. **The question:** quoted big in a soft blue box, where it was asked and
   when in grey beside it. The real words, not a summary.
2. **Today:** a red frame, a red cross in a circle and "Today:" with why it
   fails; inside, the real answer as given and a red tag ("not_covered").
3. **With the fix:** a green frame, a green tick and "With" and the fix;
   inside, the answer it would give and a green tag ("answered"). Values
   go in a small table, a line between rows.
4. **A verdict under each:** in bold, red or green, what the panel shows;
   a line under it says where the real answer was seen, or in amber what
   is still to confirm.
5. **KPI cards:** four big numbers for the whole, each a few words of what
   it counts; red or amber for a count that stands for a gap.
6. **Two lists:** "Works" with green ticks; "Missing, by effort" with a
   pill per item, red for work to do (small, medium), amber for what waits
   on an answer (wait, check, decide). The item the case is about first,
   in bold.
7. **Ticks and crosses** are drawn as paths, not typed as glyphs, so every
   font shows them alike.

03Annotated screen: where on the screen

A plain sketch of a screen, grey blocks and a few real labels, with an amber number on each spot that changes; beside it a numbered list says what changes at each. The reader sees where the change is before reading what it is.

Fits when

  • A change to a screen: a field moves, a button gets a new state, a message shows in a new place.
  • The question is where: words alone would say "the error moves up" and leave the reader to guess from where to where.
  • No screenshots yet: the change is planned, or the screen is still being built.

Not when

  • Real screenshots exist before and after: one case, the screenshots side by side.
  • The parts of a system, not of a screen: a container diagram.
  • A thing's states and what moves it between them: a state diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. The sketch: the screen as a framed wireframe, its parts as plain grey blocks; only the parts that matter get real labels, such as the total, a field's placeholder or a button's text.
  2. States: a frame per state when the change shows in one state only, such as while paying or after an error; the state's name in bold above its frame. One frame when the state does not matter.
  3. The numbers: an amber circle with a number beside each spot that changes, in the margin of the frame, never over a label; each number once only, in the frame where it shows best.
  4. Colour in the sketch: grey for what stays; the changed parts in their real colours, such as a blue button or a red error.
  5. The list: beside the sketch, the same amber numbers in order, each with what changes in bold and a line or two of why under it.
  6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence all the changes together.
In the author's words
  • Good, add them all. (2026-10-16 21:00)

# Annotated screen: where on the screen

A plain sketch of a screen, grey blocks and a few real labels, with an
amber number on each spot that changes; beside it a numbered list says
what changes at each. The reader sees where the change is before reading
what it is.

![The checkout page sketched twice, while paying and with the card declined, in grey blocks with real labels for Checkout, the total of $84.00, the coupon field and the Pay button; amber number 1 sits by the coupon field under the total, 2 by the Pay button, faded, with a spinner and the word Paying, 3 by a red Card declined message right above the blue Pay button; beside the sketches a list says 1 the coupon field moves from the top of the page to under the total, 2 Pay shows a spinner and stays disabled until the bank answers, 3 the error shows right above the button, not at the top of the page; a Now box sums up the three changes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/screen_checkout.svg)

## Fits when

- **A change to a screen:** a field moves, a button gets a new state, a
  message shows in a new place.
- **The question is where:** words alone would say "the error moves up"
  and leave the reader to guess from where to where.
- **No screenshots yet:** the change is planned, or the screen is still
  being built.

## Not when

- **Real screenshots exist** before and after: [one case](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/case.md), the
  screenshots side by side.
- **The parts of a system,** not of a screen: a
  [container diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/containers.md).
- **A thing's states** and what moves it between them: a
  [state diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/state.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **The sketch:** the screen as a framed wireframe, its parts as plain
   grey blocks; only the parts that matter get real labels, such as the
   total, a field's placeholder or a button's text.
2. **States:** a frame per state when the change shows in one state
   only, such as while paying or after an error; the state's name in
   bold above its frame. One frame when the state does not matter.
3. **The numbers:** an amber circle with a number beside each spot that
   changes, in the margin of the frame, never over a label; each number
   once only, in the frame where it shows best.
4. **Colour in the sketch:** grey for what stays; the changed parts in
   their real colours, such as a blue button or a red error.
5. **The list:** beside the sketch, the same amber numbers in order,
   each with what changes in bold and a line or two of why under it.
6. **Now:** a blue box under the panel says in one sentence all the
   changes together.

04State diagram: what moves a thing between its states

The states a thing has and what moves it from one to the next: a card's steps, a message's life, a job's run. Each state is a box; each arrow says what moves it.

Fits when

  • A thing has a few states, and the question is how it gets from one to another, or why it stays in one.
  • A state can be reached by more than one way, or left by a way that goes back.
  • A bug is a wrong state: stuck, skipped, or reached from where it should not be.

Not when

  • The order of calls between parts is the question: that is a sequence diagram.
  • One decision with its answers, no lasting state: a flowchart.
  • More than about eight states: draw the part that matters, and say the rest.

How it is drawn

  1. States: rounded boxes, a short name each. Coloured by what they mean: blue a step on the way, green the end that is wanted, orange one that needs a look.
  2. Transitions: the project's arrows, grey, each with the few words that move it (a click, an answer, a timeout).
  3. The start: a filled dot with an arrow into the first state.
  4. Around it: a title with the thing's name, one line of context, one line under it saying how to read it.
In the author's words

## Not when

- **More than about eight states:** draw the part that matters, and say the

## How it is drawn

1. **States:** rounded boxes, a short name each. Coloured by what they mean:

2. **Transitions:** the project's arrows, grey, each with the few words

3. **The start:** a filled dot with an arrow into the first state.
4. **Around it:** a title with the thing's name, one line of context, one

   grey what is known so far.
4. **Big numbers:** a row under the panels, each a number and two lines
   of what it counts; amber or red when it stands for a gap.
5. **Facts only in green:** a line in a green panel is read from the
   code or a log; a guess is a question, and goes in amber.

08Cause tree: why it happened

The failure on top, its causes below it as a tree: each row down says why the row above happened. The root cause is amber, the fix green beside it, and the causes that were checked and ruled out stay in grey with the reason. The reader sees why it broke, what one change ends it, and what was already looked at.

Fits when

  • Something broke and the question is why, down to the one cause a change would end.
  • Several causes were suspected, and the reader sees which were checked and why they are out.
  • The fix follows from the cause, and the reader sees it is aimed at the root, not at the failure on top.

Not when

  • The order of events in one request: a sequence diagram; what happened when, from a log: a timeline.
  • The cause is not found yet: what is known and what is still open, a questions diagram.
  • One real request today beside the same with the fix: a case.

How it is drawn

  1. The failure: a red box on top, what broke in a few words and, under it, how much or since when.
  2. The causes: one box per row down, each the "because" of the box above it, its name in bold in two or three words and under it what shows it; dark lines join the chain from the failure to the root.
  3. Ruled out: a grey box with a dashed border beside the cause it was checked against, its name in grey and "ruled out:" with the reason; grey dashed lines join it.
  4. The root cause: the last box of the chain, amber with an amber border, its name in bold and "the root cause" under it.
  5. The fix: a green box beside the root cause, joined to it by a green line, the change in bold.
  6. Now: a blue box under the tree says in one sentence why it broke and what fixes it.

10Chronology: what one user did, in order

Steps in the order they happened, each with its time, at even distances: the order and the times count, not the gaps between them. A long gap is cut short, its length written on the cut.

For more steps than a strip holds, the same chronology goes down a line, the times on the left, one row per step.

Fits when

  • One actor's steps: a user, a job, an agent; first this, then that.
  • The order matters more than the distances: a minute and a night between two steps take the same room.
  • Steps far apart in time: minutes, then a day, then a week; a timeline would squeeze the short ones flat.

Not when

  • The gaps are the story: a wait, a timeout, what happened while something else waited: a timeline.
  • Several parts pass something between them: a sequence diagram.
  • The states matter, not the steps: a state diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. The line: one grey line, left to right in the strip, top to bottom in the list.
  2. Steps: a dot each, at even distances. In the strip, a stem to its label, the time in bold above a few words, the labels above and below in turn; in the list, the time on the left, the words on the right.
  3. Colours: blue for each step, green for the end that is wanted, red for a step that went wrong.
  4. A long gap: the line cut by two slanted amber strokes, its length written in amber on the cut.
  5. Strip or list: a strip up to seven or eight steps; more, the list.

  4. The longest chain: its arrows bold blue, so the reader sees which parts move the end date and which can slip.
  5. Where each stands: green is done, blue under way, grey with a dashed border not started, amber with "waits on you" a part the reader must do or approve.
  6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what holds the end date, what has time to spare and what waits on the reader.

- **The question is what holds the end date:** which parts must not
  slip, and which have time to spare.
- **A part waits on the reader,** and the reader sees how much waits
  behind it.

## Not when

- **One goal's steps in a line,** one after another: a
  [milestone track](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/milestone.md).
- **The months ahead,** bars against dates: a [roadmap](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/roadmap.md).
- **Work by stage today,** not by what it waits on: a
  [kanban board](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/kanban.md).
- **What is decided where,** questions and their answers: a
  [flowchart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flowchart.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **The parts:** one box per part, its name in bold, P1, P2 and so on
   with a few words; under it how long it takes and where it stands.
   Three to eight parts.
2. **The columns:** left to right in the order the parts can start, the
   days on top. Parts that can run side by side are stacked in one
   column.
3. **The arrows:** from a part to each part that waits on it, from box
   edge to box edge, thin grey.
4. **The longest chain:** its arrows bold blue, so the reader sees which
   parts move the end date and which can slip.
5. **Where each stands:** green is done, blue under way, grey with a
   dashed border not started, amber with "waits on you" a part the
   reader must do or approve.
6. **Now:** a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what holds
   the end date, what has time to spare and what waits on the reader.

15Priority quadrant: what to do first

Many pieces of work weighed on two things only: how much each is worth and how much it costs. Value goes up, effort goes right, and the square splits in four quarters: do first, plan, later, skip. The reader sees what to start with and what to drop.

Fits when

  • Many ideas and room for a few, and the question is which ones to start with.
  • Two things decide it: what a piece of work brings and what it costs, each a rough guess, not a measure.
  • The reader must say no to some of them, and wants to see why.

Not when

  • Work by stage today, in flight or stuck: a kanban board.
  • The months ahead, what is planned when: a roadmap.
  • Options compared on many criteria, not two: a table, a row per option and a column per criterion.

How it is drawn

  1. The axes: value up the left side, effort along the bottom, each an arrow with its name; no numbers, only more and less.
  2. The quarters: four framed boxes with a gap between them, each named in its outer corner in bold, what it means under the name. Do first is green, top left; plan is blue, top right; later is grey, bottom left; skip is grey with a dashed border, bottom right.
  3. The dots: one per piece of work, where its value and effort put it, in its quarter's colour; a skipped one is hollow. Four to twelve of them.
  4. The labels: the name in bold on its own light pill beside its dot, clear of the quarter's border and of other pills; right of the dot, or left when the right has no room.
  5. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what comes first and what is dropped.

16Container sketch (C4): where the parts run

Which parts a system has, where each one runs, and what goes between them: the container level of the C4 model, drawn as a sketch.

Fits when

  • The question is where: which machine, which box, which service runs a part.
  • Something crosses a boundary: a laptop to a server, a box to the internet, and what goes across.
  • A newcomer needs the whole before any one part.

Not when

  • The order of the calls matters: a sequence diagram.
  • The data and how it links is the question: an entity-relationship diagram.
  • The inside of one part: its states or its decisions, a state diagram or a flowchart.

How it is drawn

  1. Where things run: dashed boxes with their names at the top left (a laptop, other machines, the internet).
  2. Parts: boxes inside them, a name and one line of what each is; the one the reply is about in blue.
  3. What goes between them: the project's arrows, grey, each with a few words.
  4. Names: the standard ones from the glossary of names (laptop, router, vps1, box), never a private host.

Examples

17Entity-relationship: what data there is and how it links

The kinds of data a system keeps, their main fields, and how many of one go with one of another: 1 to n, n to n, marked on each line's ends.

Fits when

  • The question is about data: where something is kept, what points to what.
  • A change touches a link: one becomes many, or a link goes away.
  • A newcomer reads the storage before the code.

Not when

  • Where the data lives (which machine, which service): a container sketch.
  • What happens to one record over time: a state diagram.
  • Every field of every table: keep the main ones; the schema is in the code.

How it is drawn

  1. Entities: a box per kind of data, its name in bold on a tinted band, its main fields under it.
  2. Links: plain lines, no arrowheads, a verb under the line (holds, has, linked in).
  3. Their ends, crow's feet: two short bars across the line where it is one, a three-pronged foot with a bar before it where it is many (one or more). 1 and n in bold beside them, for a reader who does not know the marks.
  4. Left to right in the order a reader meets them; a child under its parent.

18Status dashboard: where each part stands

A RAG status dashboard (red, amber, green): the state of many parts at once, each a tile coloured by its state. Big numbers on top, the tiles grouped below, the gaps gathered at the end. Two more kinds at the end: tiles coloured by where each part is, and a whole beside its gap.

Fits when

  • The question is where things stand: many parts, each in place, stale or missing.
  • The reader must find the gaps fast: a project's checks, a release, an audit of what is covered.
  • The same view is read again later, and the colours show what moved.

Not when

  • One thing and its states over time: a state diagram.
  • What happened in what order: a timeline or a sequence diagram.
  • A few parts only: a sentence or a list says it; a dashboard needs enough tiles to scan.

How it is drawn

  1. The key: green in place and checked, amber stale or unchecked, red missing or failed, in one line under the title.
  2. KPI cards: three or four big numbers on top, each a word of what it counts and a line of context, coloured like the worst it stands for.
  3. The status board: a panel per area, its name and a line of what it holds; a tile per part, its name in bold and its state in its colour.
  4. The gaps: the amber and red tiles again, gathered in a panel at the end, so the reader does not hunt for them.
  5. Real states only: a tile's word says why it has its colour ("1 failed", "no test"), never just "bad".

Coloured by where it is

When the question is where each part is, not how it is, the colours name places: production, development, the working tree. The list behind a tile opens on a click, in a panel beside the grid.

  1. A card per place, in the colour its tiles get: green, on production as it is; blue, on development and not released; amber, only in the working tree and not committed.
  2. Each tile in the colour of its latest change: its name in bold, a small word for what is not out yet ("not released").
  3. A red dot on a tile: a question it cannot answer, its data missing.
  4. The key under the grid, the red dot in it too.
  5. Details on a click: the chosen tile gets a dark outline; the panel beside the grid shows its name, a tag of where it is, and short sections, headed in small caps, of a few bullets each. The tile never grows to hold its list.

A whole and its gap

When the question is how much is covered, one bar shows the whole and what is missing from it; a row of squares counts the runs.

  • The bar: a segment per kind, as wide as its count, dark green, light green, a thin strip for the rest.
  • The gap: a dashed red segment at the end, hatched soft red, its label on a pill: "+ coupons, sizes".
  • A grey line under the bar names the strip and the dashed part.
  • Units as squares, in rows: filled green passed, filled red failed, empty with a red outline skipped. A grey line under them says which failed, when, and why the rest were skipped.

19Line chart: a number over time

One number over days or hours, a point for each, joined by a line; a dashed line marks the moment something changed, a deploy or a fix. The reader sees the number before and after, and whether it stayed.

Fits when

  • One number, measured again and again: a load time, an error rate, a queue's length; two numbers at most.
  • The question is before and after: did the deploy or the fix move the number, and did it stay moved.
  • A goal or a limit exists, and the reader sees which side of it the line is on.

Not when

  • One run's time by function: a flame graph.
  • When something happens by hour and day of the week: a heatmap.
  • Work planned over months: a roadmap.
  • Events from a log, not a measured number: a timeline.

How it is drawn

# Line chart: a number over time

One number over days or hours, a point for each, joined by a line; a
dashed line marks the moment something changed, a deploy or a fix. The
reader sees the number before and after, and whether it stayed.

![The checkout page's p95 load time from 10-01 to 10-14, a point a day, 0 to 3 s up the side: before the deploy the line is red at about 2.4 s, between 2.3 and 2.6; a blue dashed line marks the deploy of 10-08; after it the line is green at about 0.9 s, between 0.8 and 1.0; a grey dashed line marks the goal of 1.5 s; a Now box says the deploy cut p95 from about 2.4 s to 0.9 s, well under the goal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/linechart_checkout.svg)

## Fits when

- **One number, measured again and again:** a load time, an error rate,
  a queue's length; two numbers at most.
- **The question is before and after:** did the deploy or the fix move
  the number, and did it stay moved.
- **A goal or a limit exists,** and the reader sees which side of it the
  line is on.

## Not when

- **One run's time by function:** a [flame graph](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flame.md).
- **When something happens by hour and day of the week:** a
  [heatmap](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/heatmap.md).
- **Work planned over months:** a [roadmap](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/roadmap.md).
- **Events from a log,** not a measured number: a
  [timeline](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/timeline.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **Time:** left to right along the bottom, the dates or hours under
   it, every other one when they crowd; a week to a month of days, or a
   day of hours.
2. **The number:** up the side from zero, a few round values with their
   unit ("1 s", "2 s"), a thin line across the panel at each.
3. **The line:** a dot per measurement, joined. Red before the change,
   green after it when the number improved; one colour when nothing
   changed.
4. **The change:** a blue dashed line down the panel at its moment, its
   name and date on a blue pill at the top.
5. **The goal:** a grey dashed line across, its value at the right end;
   only when there is one.
6. **What it says:** the typical value before and after in the line's
   colour, next to the line, in a few words.
7. **Now:** a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what changed
   and by how much.

Not when

  3. The scale: on the line under the title, a swatch per step with its range, from none to the darkest.
  4. The hot spot: a blue frame around its cells, their counts inside them; under the grid, in blue, its days, its hours and its share of the whole.
  5. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence when most of it happens and why.

28Trace waterfall: where one request spends its time

One request traced across services: a row per span, each a bar from its start to its end on one scale of milliseconds, a called span indented under its caller. The reader sees the slowest span, what runs in turn, and the gaps where the request only waits.

Fits when

  • "Why is this request slow?": one request, measured across the services it passes.
  • Calls in turn or at once: the reader sees what waits for what, and what could run side by side.
  • Time lost between spans: a gap where nothing runs is as plain as the work.

Not when

  • The call stacks of one process, by function: a flame graph.
  • Who talks to whom, in order, with the messages: a sequence diagram.
  • A number over time, many requests: a line chart.

How it is drawn

  1. Time: milliseconds left to right in one framed panel, the ticks on top, faint dashed lines down from them; zero is the request's start.
  2. Rows: one per span in the order it starts, the service in bold and what it did after it; a called span indented under its caller.
  3. Milliseconds: each span's time in a column right before its bar, so the numbers read down one line.
  4. Bars: one per span from its start to its end, to one scale; a few milliseconds still get a thin bar. The slowest span is solid red, its name and time in red.
  5. Waits: a gap where no span runs is an amber band behind the rows, its length on an amber pill under them.
  6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence where the time goes.

One request traced across services: a row per span, each a bar from its
start to its end on one scale of milliseconds, a called span indented
under its caller. The reader sees the slowest span, what runs in turn,
and the gaps where the request only waits.

![A trace of POST /checkout, 1840 ms: the api's bar spans it all; under it auth checks the token in 40 ms, the cart service loads the cart in 240 ms with a database read of 180 ms indented under it, then an amber band marks 160 ms of waiting, then the payment provider charges the card in 1200 ms in red, the database saves the order in 80 ms and the mail queue takes the receipt in 30 ms; a Now box says the payment provider takes 1200 of the 1840 ms and 160 ms before it is a wait](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vbarbarosh/rules/main/img/diagrams/waterfall_checkout.svg)

## Fits when

- **"Why is this request slow?":** one request, measured across the
  services it passes.
- **Calls in turn or at once:** the reader sees what waits for what, and
  what could run side by side.
- **Time lost between spans:** a gap where nothing runs is as plain as
  the work.

## Not when

- **The call stacks of one process,** by function: a
  [flame graph](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/flame.md).
- **Who talks to whom,** in order, with the messages: a
  [sequence diagram](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/sequence.md).
- **A number over time,** many requests: a [line chart](https://github.com/vbarbarosh/rules/blob/main/diagrams/linechart.md).

## How it is drawn

1. **Time:** milliseconds left to right in one framed panel, the ticks
   on top, faint dashed lines down from them; zero is the request's
   start.
2. **Rows:** one per span in the order it starts, the service in bold
   and what it did after it; a called span indented under its caller.
3. **Milliseconds:** each span's time in a column right before its bar,
   so the numbers read down one line.
4. **Bars:** one per span from its start to its end, to one scale; a
   few milliseconds still get a thin bar. The slowest span is solid red,
   its name and time in red.
5. **Waits:** a gap where no span runs is an amber band behind the rows,
   its length on an amber pill under them.
6. **Now:** a blue box under the panel says in one sentence where the
   time goes.

29Data flow diagram: where data crosses a trust boundary

The threat modeller's view: outside parties, processes and data stores, the flows between them labelled with the data they carry, and the trust boundaries as red dashed lines. Each crossing gets a number to discuss.

Fits when

  • A security review or a threat model: each crossing is a place to ask what can go wrong (STRIDE per crossing).
  • Privacy: where personal data goes and what leaves.

Not when

  • Ports and rules: a network diagram.
  • The order of one request: a sequence diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. Notation: outside parties as boxes, processes as circles, stores as two open lines; a key.
  2. Flows: arrows named by their data ("card token"), not by protocol.
  3. Boundaries: red dashed lines; a numbered badge where a flow crosses one, the risky ones noted under the drawing.

30Dependency matrix: every link in a grid

The parts as rows and the same parts as columns; a filled cell where the row calls the column. Every link at once, however many, with no lines to cross.

Fits when

  • Many parts: where a graph turns into a hairball.
  • Layers and cycles: with the parts in order, a call below the diagonal goes against the layers.

Not when

  • A few parts: a layered diagram reads faster.
  • The order of the calls: a sequence diagram.

How it is drawn

  1. Rows and columns: the same parts in the same order, the column names turned upright, groups bracketed on the left.
  2. Cells: filled where the row calls the column, with a port or a verb when it fits.
  3. Reading: a line under it says how ("the row calls the column").

31Call graph: which function calls which

A program from its entry down: each function a box, an arrow to each one it calls, the related ones framed together, the helpers everything leans on at the bottom.

Fits when

  • A change is planned: what calls the function, what it touches.

Not when

  • What the script reads and writes: a data flow of a script.
  • Where the time goes: a flame graph.

How it is drawn

  1. Layers: the entry at the top, each call one row lower.
  2. Groups: light frames for the functions of one step.
  3. Too many: the main ones drawn, the rest a "+N more" box.

33Module graph: which file needs which

34Change map: what a change touches

The project's folder tree, trimmed to the files one change touches: each file a row, marked added, changed or removed, its lines added and removed at the right. The reader sees where the change lands and how big it is before reading the diff.

Fits when

  • One commit or one pull request: which files it adds, changes and removes, and where in the project they sit.
  • The question is where to look first: the big rows, the removed file, the one changed file in a folder of new ones.
  • A change spreads over folders: code, tests and docs, and the reader sees that each got its part.

Not when

  • Which file needs which: a module graph.
  • How big each part of the code is, not what one change did: a treemap.
  • A script's data flow, files in and files out: a pipeline.

How it is drawn

  1. The total: on top of the panel, the number of files, then how many added, changed and removed in their colours; the lines added in green and removed in red at the right.
  2. The tree: folders in bold with a slash, each level indented, thin grey lines from a folder to what it holds.
  3. The files: one row each, a mark and its name in colour: green + added, blue ~ changed, red − removed and struck through.
  4. The lines: at the right of each file, the lines added and removed as numbers, then a bar of green and red as long as they are.
  5. What it leaves alone: folders and files the change does not touch fold into one grey row, "… 4 more files" or "… bin/, public/".
  6. Now: a blue box under the panel says in one sentence what the change is and which file to check first.

35Flame graph: where one run spends its time

One measured run: each call stack a column of bars, the caller under the callee, each bar as wide as its share of the time. The widest bars at the top are where the time goes.

Fits when

  • "Why is it slow?": the time of a run by function, measured.
  • Before and after a speed fix: the same bar, narrower.

Not when

  • The structure, not the time: a call graph.
  • Time across services: a sequence diagram of a trace.

How it is drawn

  1. Bars: bottom-up, the whole run at the bottom, widths to one scale, the name and the milliseconds in each.
  2. Too narrow: a letter in the bar, its name in a key; a narrow part that matters zoomed above.
  3. Self time: the bars that spend it themselves marked in orange.
